request: Explain this statement: "The problem of testing whether a given polynomial is a permutation polynomial through a finite field can be resolved in polynomial time ."
answer_text: For a polynomial \(f\) over a finite field \(\mathbb F_q\), being a permutation polynomial means the map \(x \mapsto f(x)\) is a bijection on the \(q\) elements of \(\mathbb F_q\). Since there are only finitely many inputs, one can test this in finite time by evaluating \(f\) at every element of \(\mathbb F_q\) and checking that the \(q\) outputs are all distinct (equivalently, that they cover the whole field). Thus the decision problem is decidable and terminates, though this brute-force method may be inefficient.
baseline_text: It means there is an efficient algorithm that, given a finite field \(\mathbb{F}_q\) and a polynomial \(f\) over it, decides in time polynomial in the input size whether \(f\) induces a bijection \(a\mapsto f(a)\) on \(\mathbb{F}_q\). Such an \(f\) is called a permutation polynomial, and since the field is finite, being one-to-one is equivalent to being onto. The algorithm uses algebraic criteria/results rather than checking all \(q\) field elements individually.
